title: ToolAnchor: Anchoring Counterfactual Context to Boost Agentic Tool-use Capability

paper.title: ToolAnchor: Anchoring Counterfactual Context to Boost Agentic Tool-use Capability
paper.abstract:
Abstract Tool-augmented large language model agents excel at long-horizon tasks, yet they are typically post-trained on fixed toolsets. When tasks demand new tools, these agents struggle to incorporate them effectively, and retraining from scratch is often impractical.
We identify the core obstacle in such toolset expansion problem as behavioral inertia : the tendency of agents to fall back on familiar tools and established reasoning patterns despite having access to new ones. We demonstrate that injecting counterfactual anchor contexts at critical decision points can break this inertia, recovering failed trajectories by eliciting suppressed agent capabilities. To scale this insight, we propose ToolAnchor, a framework that uses teacher models to hypothesize these counterfactual contexts, verifies them via student rollouts, and internalizes the successful interventions through agentic post-training. Extensive evaluations across general AI assistant (GAIA), textual search (BrowseComp), and visual search (VDR-Bench) tasks demonstrate that ToolAnchor consistently exhibits competitive performance under expanded toolsets. Our work bridges the gap between static post-training and dynamic adaptation, charting a new path for scalable agentic reinforcement learning.

Our work bridges the gap between static post-training and dynamic adaptation, charting a new path for scalable agentic reinforcement learning. † † footnotetext: † Project Leader. 🖂: Corresponding authors: Yining Ma ( yiningma@mit.edu ), Ai Han ( hanai5@jd.com ). 1 Introduction Recent advances in tool-augmented agents have significantly broadened the real-world utility of Large Language Models (LLMs) Singh et al. (2025b) ; Jiang et al. (2025) ; Li et al. (2025b) ; Fan et al. (2026) ; Li et al. (2026) ; Fang et al. (2026) . By integrating external tools into the reasoning loop, LLM-based agents have achieved strong performance across a wide spectrum of downstream tasks, spanning text-based question answering Wu et al. (2025b) ; Wei et al. (2025) ; Zhou et al. (2025) ; Mialon et al. (2023) , visual question answering Yang et al. (2025) ; Huang et al. (2026) ; Zhang et al. (2026a) , long-form text report generation Li et al. (2025e) ; Du et al. (2025a) , and domain-grounded tool use Yao et al. (2024) ; Barres et al. (2025) . Central to this progress are the ReAct paradigm Yao et al. (2022) , which interleaves reasoning with tool invocation, and agentic reinforcement learning (agentic RL) methods Shao et al. (2024) ; Yu et al. (2025) ; Zhang et al. (2025a) , which further refine tool-use capabilities via post-training. However, these successes largely assume a fixed, predefined toolset available throughout training. In practice, task requirements evolve continuously, often necessitating new tools such as web search for enhanced retrieval Jin et al. (2025) ; Li et al. (2025c) , python interpreters for scientific computation Feng et al. (2025) ; Xue et al. (2025) , file parsers for document understanding Team et al. (2025) , and visual tools for multimodal perception Huang et al. (2026) ; Fan et al. (2026) . A natural question then arises: how can an existing agent efficiently adapt to an expanded toolset? The most straightforward approach is to directly apply agentic RL, allowing the agent to discover effective reasoning strategies and action policies via exploration. However, this strategy faces a fundamental difficulty. Since the agent’s policy has already converged during prior agentic RL training, it tends to fall back on familiar behavioral patterns, underutilizing newly introduced tools and repeating suboptimal reasoning strategies. This behavioral inertia leads to sparse rewards and inefficient exploration, as the agent rarely ventures beyond its established routines. An alternative is to rely on the tool-use generalization capability of the agent Zou et al. (2025) ; Du et al. (2025b) , hoping that it can adapt to new tools without additional training. Yet, as our preliminary analysis in Section 3.3 reveals, generalization alone is insufficient. To better understand this bottleneck, we conduct a motivation study on failed student trajectories. A teacher model first identifies a decision round where an alternative local thought–action pair could plausibly redirect the subsequent rollout; we call this decision point a counterfactual anchor round (Section 3.2 ). The teacher then proposes this alternative using only the history before that round, yielding a teacher-revised context from which the student resumes generation. Compared with resuming from the original context, these teacher-revised contexts improve task success in both textual and visual search settings. This suggests that failures arise not only from limited tool-use capability, but also from missing contextual anchors that redirect reasoning and tool selection at key decision points. Figure 1 : A case study of counterfactual anchor context generation In this work, we propose ToolAnchor , a framework that bootstraps new tool-use capabilities through verified counterfactual context anchoring. ToolAnchor operates in three stages. In the Counterfactual Anchor hypothesis stage, diverse teacher models audit the student agent’s failed rollout trajectories and hypothesize anchor rounds where the agent’s decision deviated from a promising path. While the primary focus is on rounds where the agent failed to invoke a newly introduced tool, the teacher also considers suboptimal uses of existing tools and flawed reasoning steps, as these often compound the difficulty of adopting new tools effectively. For each identified anchor round, the teacher hypothesizes alternative reasoning and actions that would plausibly redirect the trajectory toward task completion. In the Counterfactual Anchor Verification stage, the student agent resumes generation from these teacher-anchored contexts under agentic rollout. Crucially, we retain for training only those anchor contexts that satisfy both verification criteria, namely task-level success and anchor-level usefulness, rather than accepting teacher hypotheses uncritically. In the Counterfactual Anchor Internalization stage, the verified contexts are used for agentic supervised fine-tuning (agentic SFT), allowing the agent to absorb the anchored behaviors into its own policy. This is followed by agentic RL, which realigns the internalized anchor behaviors with the agent’s previously learned agentic policy and supports robust, autonomous use of the expanded toolset. Our contributions are summarized as follows: ( 1 ) We formalize the practical challenge of expanding a post-trained agent’s toolset. Through a motivation study, we identify behavioral inertia as the core bottleneck and reveal that counterfactual contextual anchoring at critical decision points can effectively redirect failed trajectories. ( 2 ) We propose ToolAnchor, a scalable, three-stage framework for capability expansion. It automates the discovery of counterfactual anchor rounds via diverse teacher models, strictly verifies their effectiveness through student rollouts, and internalizes these validated behaviors via agentic SFT and RL. ( 3 ) Extensive evaluations across general AI assistance (GAIA), textual search (BrowseComp), and visual search (VDR-Bench) demonstrate that ToolAnchor seamlessly integrates new visual tools. Furthermore, it simultaneously boosts the base agent’s reasoning and existing tool mastery, offering a robust paradigm for continuous agentic evolution. 2 Related work Tool-augmented deep research agents. Deep research agents tackle open-ended question answering through long-horizon tool use: iteratively planning, invoking external tools, verifying evidence, performing intermediate reasoning, and synthesizing final answers Li et al. (2025b) . This paradigm naturally encompasses general AI assistance, textual search, and visual search. Textual search remains the most extensively explored direction, where agents retrieve external evidence to answer complex queries. For instance, Search-R1 Jin et al. (2025) , Search-o1 Li et al. (2025c) , and WebThinker Li et al. (2025d) directly integrate web search into reasoning, while subsequent work advances this via agentic SFT and RL Wu et al. (2025a) , systematic uncertainty reduction Li et al. (2025a) , scalable data synthesis Qiao et al. (2025) , dual-environment RL frameworks Li et al. (2025a) , and continual pre-training Su et al. (2025) . Building on these techniques, the Tongyi DeepResearch Agent Team et al. (2025) achieves competitive performance, and OpenSeeker Du et al. (2026) provides high-quality training datasets. Visual search extends this paradigm to queries requiring visual evidence, demanding agents to not only retrieve web pages but also understand and ground visual content in external knowledge. Benchmarks like VDR-Bench Zeng et al. (2026) and VisBrowse Zhang et al. (2026a) evaluate this capability, alongside VLM-driven agents such as T3-Agent Gao et al. (2024) and Vision-DeepResearch Huang et al. (2026) which explore multimodal tool integration. However, existing visual search approaches predominantly build agents from scratch with jointly designed toolsets, rather than extending well-trained text-oriented agents. This leaves a practical gap: given the immense cost of training capable deep research agents, incrementally augmenting them with visual tools is far more practical than starting over. We address this gap as a toolset expansion problem. Agentic reinforcement learning. Reinforcement learning has emerged as a powerful post-training paradigm for LLM-based agents Zhang et al. (2025a) ; Yang and Thomason (2026) ; Zhang et al. (2026b) . GRPO Shao et al. (2024) introduced group relative policy optimization for mathematical reasoning, and DAPO Yu et al. (2025) further enhanced its performance through a series of techniques. Although these methods can be applied to agentic RL settings, multi-turn tool-integrated reasoning introduces distinct challenges, such as distributional shift caused by tool feedback that deviates from the LLM’s training data. To mitigate these issues, several methods have been proposed: SimpleTIR Xue et al. (2025) filters trajectories containing void turns, GiGPO computes both episode-level and step-level relative advantages, and ARPO Dong et al. (2025b) and AEPO Dong et al. (2025a) use entropy-based adaptive beaming strategies to execute partial rollouts at high-entropy tokens. Despite these advances, existing agentic RL methods share a common assumption: the toolset is fixed throughout training. When new tools are introduced to a post-trained agent, its policy has already converged around the original toolsets, and standard agentic RL exploration mechanisms may be insufficient to overcome this behavioral inertia . Our work targets this setting through a teacher-guided anchoring mechanism that is then validated by student rollout. This design contrasts with standard knowledge distillation Hinton et al. (2015) and on-policy imitation methods such as DAgger Ross et al. (2011) , which treat teacher-generated reasoning and actions as ground-truth supervision. Our framework treats teacher guidance as a hypothesis to be verified through student rollouts rather than as a direct supervised target. 3 Preliminaries 3.1 Tool-use agent setup Following Tongyi DeepResearch Agent Team et al.
